title: RISC-V: Registers, Arithmetic, and Shifts
summary: This unit explores the modular RISC-V ISA (modulare RISC-V-ISA), register conventions (Registerkonventionen), and signed and unsigned arithmetic (signed- und unsigned-Arithmetik). You will learn how multiplication, division, and shifts (Shifts) change bit patterns, and which pseudo-instructions (Pseudobefehle) and immediate operations (Immediate-Operationen) are used for them. The unit concludes with common errors in assembly programming.
keyFacts: `RV32` denotes a RISC-V variant with 32-bit-wide registers; `I` stands for the base integer ISA, and `M` for multiplication and division.
`RV32I` has 32 registers, from `x0` to `x31`, each 32 bits wide.
`x0` always returns the value zero; no initial value should be assumed for any other register.
Register names such as `a0`, `s0`, and `t0` are usage conventions; they do not indicate different types of registers.
`mul` returns the lower 32 product bits; `mulh`, `mulhu`, and `mulhsu` return upper product bits using different signedness interpretations.
`div` and `rem` operate on signed values; `divu` and `remu` operate on unsigned values.
For a left shift, `sll` and `slli` fill the vacated right-hand positions with zeros; for a logical right shift, `srl` and `srli` fill the vacated left-hand positions with zeros.
For an arithmetic right shift, `sra` and `srai` fill the vacated left-hand positions with copies of the sign bit.
A one-bit left shift is guaranteed to correspond to multiplication by 2 only if the result fits in the chosen word width.
For negative odd numbers, an arithmetic right shift can differ from signed division because division rounds toward zero.
A pseudo-instruction is not a separate machine instruction; the assembler translates it into real instructions.
Depending on the constant, `li` can require different numbers of real instructions; for large constants, `lui` and `addi` are possible, for example.
An immediate is a constant included directly in the instruction.
Sign extension must be taken into account for negative immediates.
When programming in assembly, check register values, signs, loop execution, and register usage step by step.

review.notes: Ein Distraktor in der RV32I-Frage war mehrdeutig, weil Multiplikation und Division als Erweiterung M verstanden werden konnten; er wurde eindeutig als falsche Basiszuordnung formuliert. Alle 42 Fragen wurden geprüft; Rechenwerte, Antwortmengen, Quellenüberschriften und Formalia sind konsistent.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes `RV32I`?

options.text: A 32-bit variant whose base includes multiplication and division
A 64-bit variant with the base integer ISA
A 32-bit variant with the base integer ISA
A 32-bit variant with a floating-point base

questions.explanation: `RV32` denotes 32-bit registers, and `I` stands for the base integer ISA. Multiplication and division belong to the `M` extension.

questions.prompt: Select all correct matches. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `I` stands for the base integer ISA.

questions.explanation: `I` denotes the base integer ISA, `M` multiplication and division, and `F` floating point. `A` stands for atomic operations, and `V` for vector operations.

questions.prompt: `RV32I` has 32 registers, from `x0` to `x31`, and each register is 32 bits wide.
questions.explanation: The registers run from `x0` to `x31`, so there are 32 registers. In `RV32I`, each register is 32 bits wide.

questions.prompt: Register `x0` always returns ___.
questions.explanation: `x0` is the zero register and always returns the value zero, regardless of other instructions.

questions.prompt: What do names such as `a0`, `s0`, and `t0` mean in RISC-V?

options.text: They are fixed hardware types with different arithmetic.
They are alternative names for machine instructions.
They are usage conventions for registers.
They denote three different register widths.

questions.explanation: The names describe common roles, such as argument, saved, or temporary registers. They are still ordinary registers.

questions.prompt: What information does `mul` return for 32-bit operands?

options.text: The lower 32 bits of the product
The upper 32 bits of an unsigned product
The upper 32 bits of a signed product

questions.explanation: `mul` returns the lower part of the product. Use `mulh`, `mulhu`, or `mulhsu` for the upper product bits.

source.heading: Multiplikation und Division: signed oder unsigned?

questions.prompt: Select all correct matches. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `mulhu` returns the lower product bits for two unsigned operands.
`mulhsu` interprets the first operand as signed and the second as unsigned.
`mulh` returns upper product bits for two signed operands.

questions.explanation: `mulh` is signed/signed, `mulhsu` is signed/unsigned, and `div` and `rem` operate on signed values. `mulhu` returns upper, not lower, product bits; `divu` and `remu` are unsigned.

questions.prompt: How does `srl` fill the positions vacated on the left by a right shift?

options.text: With copies of the sign bit

questions.explanation: `srl` is a logical right shift and fills the left-hand positions with zeros. Copying the sign bit is done by `sra`.

questions.prompt: A pseudo-instruction is a machine instruction with its own separate opcode.
questions.explanation: A pseudo-instruction is only a readable assembly notation. The assembler translates it into one or more real machine instructions.

questions.prompt: An immediate is a ___ included directly in the instruction.
questions.explanation: An immediate is a fixed numeric value contained in the instruction; it is not read from a register.

questions.prompt: For `t0 = 0x2C`, which operation keeps only the lower four bits?
questions.explanation: `andi` with the mask `0x0F` sets all higher bits to zero and keeps only the lower four bits.

questions.prompt: Which extensions are included in `RV32IM`?

options.text: 32-bit registers, the base integer ISA, and multiplication/division
64-bit registers, the base integer ISA, and floating point

questions.explanation: `RV32` specifies the register width, `I` denotes the base integer ISA, and `M` adds multiplication and division.

questions.prompt: The 4-bit patterns `1101` and `0010` are multiplied as signed values. What 8-bit result is produced?
questions.explanation: As signed values, `1101` is −3 and `0010` is 2. Their product is −6, represented as `1111 1010`.

questions.prompt: The 4-bit patterns `0110` and `0101` are multiplied as unsigned numbers. The complete product is represented with 8 bits. Which bit pattern is produced?
questions.explanation: As unsigned values, the operands are 6 and 5. Their product is 30, which is represented by the 8-bit pattern `0001 1110`.

questions.prompt: Which instruction computes a quotient using a signed interpretation?
questions.explanation: `div` returns the signed quotient. `divu` is the unsigned variant; `rem` and `remu` return the remainder.

questions.prompt: Compute the 8-bit left shift `0010 1100 << 1`.
questions.explanation: In a left shift, the bits move one position to the left and a 0 is added on the right. This gives `0101 1000`, or 88.

questions.prompt: Compute the logical right shift `1101 0000 >> 1`.
questions.explanation: A logical right shift adds a 0 on the left. `1101 0000` becomes `0110 1000`, which is 104 as an unsigned value.

questions.prompt: Compute the arithmetic right shift `1101 0000 >> 1`.
questions.explanation: The sign bit 1 is copied to the left. This produces `1110 1000`, which represents −24 in 8-bit two's complement.

questions.prompt: Which sequence of real instructions can replace `not t0, t1`?
questions.explanation: XOR with a bit mask of all ones flips every bit. Therefore, `not` expands to `xori t0, t1, -1`.

questions.prompt: For `t0 = 0x2C`, what value does `ori t2, t0, 0x10` produce?
For `t0 = 0x2C`, what value does `addi t1, t0, 4` produce?
questions.explanation: `0x2C` is 44. Adding 4 gives 48, or `0x30`.

questions.prompt: A one-bit left shift is guaranteed to correspond to multiplication by 2, with the correct mathematical result, only if that result fits in the chosen word width.
questions.explanation: The bit operation itself is always the same, but a left shift discards bits that leave the word. In that case, the bit pattern no longer represents the complete product.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Names such as `a0` and `t0` are usage conventions.
An initial value of zero may be assumed for every register except `x0`.

questions.explanation: Only `x0` is guaranteed to be zero. No initial value is assumed for other registers; their names describe common roles.

questions.prompt: How do you obtain the complete 64-bit product of two signed 32-bit operands?

options.text: Lower bits with `mul`, upper bits with `mulhu`
Lower bits with `mulh`, upper bits with `mul`
Lower bits with `mul`, upper bits with `mulh`

questions.explanation: `mul` returns the lower part of the product. For two signed operands, `mulh` returns the corresponding upper part.

questions.prompt: Consider the 4-bit patterns `1101` and `0011`. Multiply them as unsigned numbers and as signed 4-bit two's-complement numbers; give both complete products using 8 bits. Statement: For these operands, the lower 4 bits of the products are the same, while the upper 4 bits differ. Is the statement true or false?
questions.explanation: As unsigned values, the patterns give $13\cdot3=39$, or `0010 0111`. In 4-bit two's complement they are $-3$ and $3$; the product $-9$ is `1111 0111` in 8-bit two's complement. Both products end in `0111`, but their upper 4 bits are `0010` and `1111`.

questions.prompt: For true division by 2 of negative odd signed values, use ___ instead of an arithmetic right shift.
questions.explanation: An arithmetic right shift can round down for negative odd numbers. `div` performs signed division with rounding toward zero.

questions.prompt: `1101 0001` is −47 as a signed value. Which combination of shift and division by 2 is correct?
questions.explanation: The arithmetic shift gives `1110 1000`, or −24. Signed division of −47 by 2 rounds toward zero and gives −23.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about shift instructions. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: `sra` fills the left-hand positions with copies of the sign bit.
The suffix `i` indicates the immediate variant.
The shift amount can be in a register or directly in the instruction.
`srl` fills the left-hand positions with copies of the sign bit.

questions.explanation: Variants without `i` use a register; variants with `i` use an immediate. `sra` preserves the sign, whereas `srl` inserts zeros on the left.

questions.prompt: Which statement about `li` is correct?

options.text: `li` can load only the value zero.
`li` is always exactly one machine instruction.
`li` is a real instruction in the M extension.
Depending on the constant, `li` may require several real instructions.

questions.explanation: For small constants, one `addi` is often enough; larger constants can be constructed using, for example, `lui` and `addi`. Therefore, `li` does not always expand to the same number of instructions.

questions.prompt: For negative immediates, I must account for ___.
questions.explanation: A negative immediate is sign-extended to the register width. This preserves its signed meaning and the correct upper bits.

questions.prompt: At the start of an assembly program, all registers except `x0` may be assumed to contain zero.
questions.explanation: Only `x0` is guaranteed to return zero. The initial value of every other register is unknown unless it has been initialized.

questions.prompt: Which check directly helps prevent loops from running one iteration too many or too few?

options.text: Check the start, termination condition, and number of iterations

questions.explanation: The loop length depends on the initial state, the termination condition, and the actual number of iterations. The other checks do not directly address this issue.

questions.prompt: Select all useful practices when programming in assembly. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Plan the flow and register usage before writing the code.
Always treat uninitialized registers as zero.
Trace the program instruction by instruction and check register values.

questions.explanation: Planning, comments, and checking the code step by step make it easier to follow and help with debugging. Uninitialized registers, however, must not automatically be treated as zero.

questions.prompt: An assembly program uses the pseudo-instruction `neg`. Which statement correctly describes the relationship between the ISA and a pseudo-instruction?

options.text: The ISA describes only register conventions, not machine instructions.
`neg` automatically extends the hardware with a new opcode.
Pseudo-instructions belong only to the operating system layer and are not translated.
The ISA defines real machine instructions; the assembler replaces `neg` with those instructions.

questions.explanation: The ISA defines the executable machine instructions. `neg` is only a readable notation and is expanded into real instructions, for example `sub t0, x0, t1`.

questions.prompt: Which bit sequence is in a 32-bit register after `addi t0, x0, -1`?
questions.explanation: `x0` returns zero. The negative immediate is sign-extended, so −1 is represented in 32 bits as `0xFFFFFFFF`.

questions.prompt: For `ld a1, 8(s0)`, the effective address is ...
questions.explanation: For a load, `a1` is the destination register. The memory address is formed from the base register `s0` and the offset 8.

questions.prompt: An 8-bit pattern `1101 0000` is shifted one position to the right. Select all correct statements. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Both instructions produce the same bit pattern.
`srai` fills the left-hand positions with zeros.

questions.explanation: `srli` inserts a 0 on the left; `srai` copies the sign bit 1. This produces different bit patterns and interpretations.

questions.explanation: As unsigned values, 13 · 2 = 26, or `0001 1010`. As signed values, −3 · 2 = −6, or `1111 1010`.

questions.explanation: `mulhsu` is designed for a signed first operand and an unsigned second operand. `mul` returns only the lower product bits, regardless of signedness.

questions.prompt: Which sequence of real instructions implements the pseudo-instruction `neg t0, t1`?
questions.explanation: Since `x0` always returns zero, `sub t0, x0, t1` computes 0 − `t1`, producing its negative.

questions.prompt:
Given `t0 = 0x2C`. Execute the three instructions; each reads the unchanged value from `t0` and writes to its own destination register:

- `ori t1, t0, 0x10`
- `xori t2, t0, 0x0F`
- `andi t3, t0, 0x0F`

Which result line is entirely correct? Results are given in hexadecimal.
questions.explanation: `0x2C OR 0x10 = 0x3C`, `0x2C XOR 0x0F = 0x23`, and `0x2C AND 0x0F = 0x0C`. All three instructions read the given value from `t0`.

questions.prompt: When checking an assembly program, select all correct practices. More than one answer may be correct.

options.text: Determine whether the signed or unsigned interpretation applies before calculating.
Assume `t0` and `t1` are zero without initializing them.
Check the starting point, termination condition, and number of loop iterations.
Check the affected register values after each relevant instruction.

questions.explanation: Signedness, register values, and loop conditions are common sources of errors. Only `x0`, not `t0` or `t1`, is automatically zero.

questions.prompt: The 8-bit pattern `1101 0000` is shifted one position to the left. Which statement correctly describes the result?

options.text: The pattern is `1010 0000`; as signed it represents −96 and as unsigned 160.
The pattern is `1010 0000`; as signed and unsigned it represents 416.
The pattern is `0110 1000`; as unsigned it represents 104.
The pattern is `1110 1000`; as signed it represents −24.

questions.explanation: The shift produces `1010 0000`. This pattern can be interpreted as signed −96 or unsigned 160; the complete unsigned product 208 · 2 = 416 does not fit in 8 bits.

questions.prompt: If the result of the unsigned left shift of `1101 0000` is the bit pattern `1010 0000`, which represents the value 160, no overflow occurred.
questions.explanation: The bit pattern does represent 160 within 8 bits, but the complete product is 208 · 2 = 416 and does not fit in 8 bits. The leftmost bit, or additional product bits, were lost.

questions.prompt: Your smartwatch packs eight yes/no states into one byte. Which operations are commonly used with a bit field like this?

options.text: Set a flag with `OR` without clearing other set bits
Isolate an arbitrary flag directly with `div`
Read an individual status flag with `AND`

questions.explanation: Bitwise logical operations are ideal for compact status fields: `AND` masks, `OR` sets, and `XOR` toggles individual bits. You will encounter these patterns in devices, protocols, and drivers.

questions.prompt: In a game, a score is stored as an 8-bit unsigned value. You want to double it with a one-bit left shift. When is this guaranteed to be a true doubling?

options.text: Only if an arithmetic right shift follows
Always, because shifting cannot cause overflow
Only if the most significant bit was 1 beforehand
Only if the mathematical result fits in 8 bits

questions.explanation: A left shift fills the right-hand positions with zeros, but discards bits that leave on the left. It is therefore guaranteed to correspond to multiplication by 2 only if the result fits in the word width.

source.heading: Links um eine Stelle: Multiplikation mit 2

questions.prompt: A sensor protocol reserves 12 bits for a measurement value. How many different bit patterns can this field represent?
questions.explanation: Each of the 12 bits can be 0 or 1: 2^12 = 4096 different bit patterns.

questions.prompt: A temperature sensor returns the signed value −47. Your code must divide by 2 using integer division and round toward zero. Which RISC-V instruction is appropriate?
questions.explanation: The signed `div` instruction from the M extension rounds −47 divided by 2 toward zero and returns −23. An arithmetic right shift instead gives −24 because it rounds down for negative values.

questions.prompt: When assembling `li t0, 100000`, you want to estimate how many instructions your program actually executes. Which statement is realistic?

options.text: `li` is a pseudo-instruction and may expand to several real instructions, depending on the constant
`li` is always exactly one machine instruction

questions.explanation: `li` is only a readable shorthand. For larger constants, the assembler may generate `lui` and `addi`, for example, so the expansion depends on the specific number.

questions.prompt: An 8-bit game counter contains the unsigned value 208. What value remains in the 8-bit register after a one-bit left shift?
questions.explanation: 208 corresponds to the bit pattern 11010000. After `<< 1`, the result is 10100000, or 160. The mathematical product 416 does not fit in 8 bits, so the leftmost bit is discarded.

source.heading: Links um eine Stelle: Multiplikation mit 2

questions.prompt: Is this correct? In a network packet, the lower four bits of a status field are flags. `andi` with the mask `0x0F` can isolate these four bits without including the upper bits in the result.
questions.explanation: A bitwise AND with `0x0F` preserves only the lower four bits; all other result bits are zero. This is a typical use of immediate masks.

questions.prompt: How many different 32-bit bit patterns can a writable data register in RV32 store?
questions.explanation: A writable RV32 data register has 32 bits. Each bit can be 0 or 1, so there are 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 different bit patterns. The register `x0`, which is hardwired to zero, is not meant here.

questions.prompt: You are reading a RISC-V function from a library: a result is returned in `a0`, while `s0` must be preserved across a function call. What explains this?

options.text: The two names automatically trigger multiplication by 2
`a0` and `s0` are hardware register types different from `x0` through `x31`
Every register starts automatically with the value zero
Register conventions for arguments, return values, and saved registers

questions.explanation: `a0` and `s0` are alternative names for registers with agreed-upon roles. These conventions help compilers, libraries, and subroutines work together, but do not change the register hardware.

questions.prompt: A big-integer library, for example one used in cryptography, multiplies two unsigned 32-bit chunks and needs the complete 64-bit product. Which statements apply?

options.text: `mulh` is always correct because signedness does not matter for the upper bits
`mulhu` returns the upper 32 product bits for two unsigned operands
`mul` alone is always enough because two 32-bit numbers produce at most 32 product bits

questions.explanation: A complete product is formed by combining the lower bits from `mul` with the corresponding upper bits. For unsigned chunks, `mulhu` from the M extension returns the upper bits; the signedness interpretation is therefore important.
